opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, the initial choices were much less magical than people might assume. In Hope, the MLP blocks form what we call a continuum memory system. Instead of a single feedforward layer that's frozen after pre-training, there's a chain of MLP blocks, each updating at its own frequency. The intuition comes from the nested learning view: every component in the model is an associative memory compressing its own context flow, and what really distinguishes them is how often they update.

So the first design question was: what range of timescales do we want to cover? At one extreme, attention or the fast memory updates at every token, so it's essentially working memory. At the other extreme, the slowest block behaves like traditional pre-trained weights, holding persistent knowledge that barely moves. The MLP blocks in between should fill that spectrum.

In practice, we spaced the frequencies roughly geometrically. Each level updates every C tokens or chunks, and the next level updates some multiple of that less often. That spacing was partly inspired by the brain. Neuroscience describes oscillations at different bands, with faster circuits handling immediate processing and slower ones supporting consolidation. We didn't try to copy specific brain rhythms. We just borrowed the principle of having multiple timescales instead of two extremes.

There were also practical constraints. The chunk sizes had to fit the sequence lengths we trained on. If the slowest in-context level never updates within a sequence, it's effectively just another static layer. The updates also have to parallelize well on hardware, which pushed us toward chunk-wise updates rather than arbitrary schedules.

So I'd call the initial values reasonable defaults. They followed a principle, but they weren't optimized. We ran some ablations, and the main finding was that having several levels of frequency matters more than the exact numbers. Even so, I think learning the frequencies, or making them adaptive to the data, is a very interesting open direction. Ideally the model decides for itself how fast each memory should change.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, the initial frequencies were a mix of principle and pragmatism. The principle comes straight from the Continuum Memory System idea: we wanted a spectrum of memory blocks, each updating at a different rate, so that fast blocks capture what's happening in the current context and slower blocks consolidate more persistent knowledge. If every MLP updated every token, you'd just have one memory with one timescale, and you lose the whole point. If they all updated too rarely, you'd basically be back to a frozen feed-forward network.

So we started with a geometric spacing. One block updates every chunk, the next every few chunks, then something like an order of magnitude slower, and so on. That's loosely inspired by how the brain seems to work, with different consolidation rhythms layered on top of each other, but I'd be careful not to over-sell the biological analogy. The real reason it's geometric is that it gives you coverage across timescales with very few blocks, and it keeps the compute overhead manageable, because the slow blocks almost never run their update step.

Then the pragmatic side: we ran small-scale sweeps. We looked at how often the self-modifying Titans core was actually writing meaningful updates, and we tuned the chunk sizes so the fastest block was in sync with that, and the slower ones were spaced so each one saw a genuinely different statistical picture of the data. If two blocks had frequencies that were too close, they'd end up learning almost redundant things, and you could see that in the ablations. The spread mattered more than the exact numbers.

One thing I want to be upfront about: we didn't do an exhaustive search over those frequencies, and I don't think our choices are optimal. A natural next step, and one we're excited about, is making the frequencies themselves learned or data-dependent, so the model decides how fast each level of memory should move. That's really where the nested learning view points you. The update schedule is just another level in the nest, and in principle it should be learnable too.

The idea was to give the MLP blocks different timescales: some update frequently and adapt to new information quickly, while others update less frequently and retain information over a longer period. So the initial choice was a design decision, rather than something the model learned. How to learn those frequencies—and make them depend on the data—is a natural next question.
